planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; European spindle tree grows readily on a wide range of soils, including chalky and clay ground, once established.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it room to develop into a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree over time. Euonymus europaeus is a Eurasian relative of the invasive Asian burning bush, grown for the same kind of dramatic autumn fruit display: in fall, four-lobed, bright pink to rose-red capsules split open along the branches to reveal glossy orange seeds, hanging on the bare stems well into winter and drawing robins and other fruit-eating birds. Small, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers in late spring give way to that fruit show, and the foliage often turns a modest yellow to reddish-purple before dropping. Because this species can self-sow into woodland edges in parts of the northeastern US, site it away from natural areas and consider the native Euonymus atropurpureus (eastern wahoo), already in this dataset, where a hedgerow-scale native alternative is preferred.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Manhattan holds its glossy foliage through most winters in zones 6 and warmer but may drop leaves and rebound from the roots after a hard freeze farther north in its range.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Manhattan is a selection of spreading euonymus valued for its dense, rounded habit and thick, glossy, dark-green leaves that hold their color and gloss better through summer heat than plain Euonymus japonicus. Small, fragrant white flowers in late summer are followed by pinkish capsules that split to reveal orange-red seeds, adding a modest fall accent to what is primarily grown as a tough, fast, low-maintenance hedge or screening plant. It tolerates shearing well and recovers quickly from hard pruning, making it a dependable choice for foundation plantings and property-line screens where a semi-evergreen backdrop is wanted. Watch for euonymus scale, which can build up on crowded or stressed plants, and treat promptly with horticultural oil if it appears.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full shade to full sun in spring; Coloratus roots wherever its trailing stems touch moist soil, so give it room to spread as a weed-suppressing mat beneath trees or on slopes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full shade to full sun; Coloratus is the classic purple-leaf selection of winter creeper, grown as a low, trailing groundcover rather than for its climbing habit. Its glossy, oval, dark-green summer leaves turn a rich plum-purple to bronze through the cold months, giving beds and slopes a distinct winter color that most broadleaf evergreen groundcovers lack. It roots as it spreads, quickly closing into a dense, weed-suppressing mat under trees or on banks too shaded and dry for turf, and tolerates drought, poor soil, and air pollution once established. As with other winter creeper cultivars, check local invasive listings before planting near natural woodland edges, since the species can escape cultivation in parts of the eastern US.

common_name: Heavy Berry Beautyberry (Exceptionally Fruitful Japanese Beautyberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Heavy Berry sets a noticeably larger fruit crop than typical seedling Japanese beautyberry, with best flowering and fruiting where it gets several hours of direct sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade. Heavy Berry is a selection of Japanese beautyberry chosen specifically for its exceptionally heavy fruit set, producing so many tight rings of metallic violet-purple berries along its arching stems each fall that they nearly obscure the wood beneath them, a step up from the already showy display of the straight species. Small pink to white flowers appear in early to midsummer ahead of the fruit, which ripens from October into early winter and persists on the bare stems as a reliable food source for songbirds after leaf drop. Like other beautyberries it flowers and fruits on new wood, so cutting stems back hard to about 6 inches in late winter each year keeps the shrub compact and promotes the heaviest berry set the following fall.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; black beautyberry is root-hardy into zone 8b but may freeze back to the ground in hard winters, resprouting vigorously from the base the following spring.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; black beautyberry is native from Mexico south through Central America into South America and has proven well adapted as an introduced ornamental in the warmest parts of the southern US, thriving in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast gardens better than most other beautyberry species. In late summer and fall it produces the same rings of clustered berries along arching stems as its American and Asian relatives, but the fruit ripens to a glossy black to deep purple-black rather than the more familiar magenta or violet, a striking, unusual color break for the genus. Small pink to lavender flowers in summer draw pollinators before the berries form, and the heavy fruit crop that follows feeds a range of songbirds into winter. Give it space to develop into a large, arching, fountain-shaped shrub, and expect occasional dieback to the roots in the coldest winters at the northern edge of its range.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Vanderbilt University Center for Latin American, Caribbean, and Latinx Studies
